vintage: 2020; 59 survey experiments during the 2016 presidential campaign
table: Results text and the average-effect table
title: Coppock, Hill and Vavreck, 'The small effects of political advertising are small regardless of context, message, sender, or receiver: Evidence from 59 real-time randomized experiments', Science Advances 6(36):eabc4046
universe: About 34,000 U.S. adults shown one of 49 campaign advertisements or a placebo
limits: One advertisement seen once, not a speech heard in person; favorability is a 1 to 5 scale. The game's stance strength runs 0 to 1, so the band below divides the scale points by the scale's width (4); that mapping is this file's assumption, not the paper's. This is the outcome band a played year checks how far one speech moves a listener against; it is not a weight any engine reads.

favorabilityEffect.quote: On average, the advertisements moved target candidate favorability 0.049 scale points (1 to 5 scale) in the “correct” direction
favorabilityEffect.heterogeneityQuote: We estimate an average treatment effect of presidential advertising on candidate favorability of 0.05 scale points on a five-point scale, with an SD across experiments of 0.07 scale points.

voteChoiceEffect.quote: The effect on target candidate vote choice is also small at 0.7 percentage points, but is not statistically significant.

stanceChangePerMessage.unit: stance strength (0 to 1) per message heard
stanceChangePerMessage.derivation: 0.049 / 4 = 0.012; the band runs from 0 to the mean plus one SD across experiments, (0.049 + 0.07) / 4 = 0.030
